topics.title: 1.1 What were the causes and immediate consequences of the 1789 Revolution?

outcomes.text: Describe absolute monarchy, royal government and the Estate system, including Third Estate discontent.
Explain the pressures for change: the American War of Independence, the Enlightenment and financial problems under Necker, Turgot and Calonne.
Explain the 1787-89 crisis: the Assembly of Notables, Parlement of Paris, bad harvests, price rises and Necker's return.
Explain the calling of the Estates-General, the cahiers, the National Assembly, the Tennis Court Oath and Louis' refusal to reform.
Describe the Storming of the Bastille and the Great Fear.
Describe the August Decrees and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.
Explain the March of the Women.

topics.title: 1.2 How and why did France become a republic by 1792?

outcomes.text: Describe the aims of revolutionary groups: Jacobins, Feuillants and Girondins.
Explain why counter-revolutionary groups failed.
Describe financial reforms, including assignats and tax reform.
Describe reforms of local government, justice and the Church.
Explain political instability: disagreement on the constitution, the King's behaviour, the flight to Varennes and the Champ de Mars.
Explain the Legislative Assembly and the declaration of war on Austria in April 1792.
Explain the September Massacres, the National Convention and abolition of the monarchy.

topics.title: 1.3 How well was France governed in the period 1793-99?

outcomes.text: Explain problems after Louis XVI's execution: sans-culottes, divisions in the Convention and war.
Describe the 1793 constitution and the Committee of Public Safety.
Explain Robespierre and the reign of terror, and economic problems.
Explain the White Terror and the Parisian risings of 1795.
Describe the Constitution of the Year III and the Directory's aims.
Explain the problems facing the Directory.
Assess the Directory's financial, military and political successes and failures.

topics.title: 1.4 What caused the rise and fall of Napoleon Bonaparte?

outcomes.text: Describe Napoleon's military reputation and political ambitions.
Explain the coup of 1799 and his initiatives as first consul.
Explain how he established authoritarian control: ministries, police, judiciary, propaganda, censorship, elections and the 1804 Empire.
Describe his legal, educational, financial and economic reforms, and the Concordat.
Explain his declining popularity at home, including conscription and the economy.
Explain the failure of the Continental System and the Peninsular War, and growing nationalism.
Explain the Russian campaign failure, defeat at Leipzig, the capture of Paris and abdication in 1814.

units.title: Papers 1 and 2 Modern Europe, 1774-1924: 2 Liberalism and nationalism in Germany, 1815-71

topics.title: 2.1 What were the causes of the Revolutions of 1848?

outcomes.text: Describe the Congress of Vienna and the Confederation's strengths and weaknesses.
Explain Metternich's system in the German states, including the Carlsbad Decrees.
Describe the aims of Liberals, the emergence of the middle class and support for liberalism in Prussia.
Explain the impact of the 1830 revolutions and support for nationalism in universities.
Describe reactions to nationalism, such as the Six Articles and Ten Articles, and the growth of nationalism in the 1840s.
Explain the economic and political impact of the Prussian Customs Union, the Zollverein and railways.
Explain the economic crisis of 1846-47, urbanisation and industrialisation's effect on skilled workers.

topics.title: 2.2 What happened during the 1848-49 revolutions and what were their consequences?

outcomes.text: Describe the spread of revolution: the fall of Metternich, revolution in Prussia and Friedrich Wilhelm IV's role.
Describe the Frankfurt Parliament's formation, actions and reasons for collapse.
Explain the impact of the 1848 revolutions.
Explain why Austrian control was reasserted: conservative strength and revolutionary divisions.
Explain changing Austria-Prussia relations after 1848 and the humiliation of Olmutz.
Explain economic issues: Zollverein disputes, Prussian growth and Austria's financial problems.
Explain political issues: liberalism, Prussia's international position and Bismarck's role to 1859.

topics.title: 2.3 Why was Bismarck appointed as Minister-President and what were his aims in the period up to 1866?

outcomes.text: Explain the Constitutional Crisis: Wilhelm I's accession, army reform proposals, Liberal reaction and the German Progressive Party.
Explain Bismarck's appointment and how he resolved the crisis.
Describe the Congress of Princes in 1863 and relations with Austria.
Explain the causes, Bismarck's involvement and outcome of the 1864 war with Denmark, including the Convention of Gastein.
Describe preparation for war: Biarritz, the secret alliance with Italy.
Explain why war broke out, including Bismarck's constitutional proposal and Austria's violation of Gastein.
Explain the outcome of the Seven Weeks' War: Treaty of Prague, the North German Confederation and the Indemnity Bill.

topics.title: 2.4 How and why was German unification achieved by 1871?

outcomes.text: Explain nationalist pressure to complete unification.
Explain the problem of the southern states, including the Zollparlament and lack of political unity.
Explain Napoleon III's ambitions and the Luxemburg Crisis.
Explain the Hohenzollern candidature, the Ems Telegram and France's declaration of war.

subtopics.title: The Franco-Prussian War and the Empire

outcomes.text: Explain why Bismarck was in a strong position: French isolation, Moltke's army and the victory at Sedan.
Describe the armistice and the Treaty of Frankfurt.
Describe the creation of the German Empire: concessions to the south, Wilhelm as Kaiser and the new constitution.

units.title: Papers 1 and 2 Modern Europe, 1774-1924: 3 Russia from autocracy to revolution, 1881-1924

topics.title: 3.1 What challenges faced the Tsarist regime in the years 1881-94?

outcomes.text: Describe autocracy: the role of the Tsar, State Council, ministries, army and Church.
Explain reform and repression under Alexander III, including Russification.
Explain economic developments: Bunge's policies, industrialisation, taxation and famines.
Explain social change, urban growth and the middle class, and opposition from peasants, workers and Marxism.

topics.title: 3.2 What were the causes and outcomes of the 1905 Revolution up to 1914?

outcomes.text: Explain the causes: discontent with Nicholas II, lack of reform and opposition from the SRs and Social Democrats.
Explain economic problems: bad harvests, unemployment, Witte's policies and taxation.
Explain the effect of defeat in the Russo-Japanese War.
Describe Bloody Sunday, strikes and unrest, and Nicholas II's response with the October Manifesto and the Duma.
Explain why the Tsarist regime survived: limited opposition, the Fundamental Laws and Dumas, and repression.
Assess change by 1914, including Stolypin's agrarian reforms and industrial developments.

topics.title: 3.3 How and why did the Bolsheviks seize power in October 1917?

outcomes.text: Explain the impact of First World War defeats and government weaknesses on the Tsar.
Explain the causes and effects of the February Revolution, including inflation, food shortages and land seizures.
Describe the events of February 1917 leading to the Tsar's abdication.
Describe the Provisional Government's formation and aims.
Explain why it failed: the war, land reform, the July Days and the Kornilov Revolt.
Explain how the Bolsheviks seized power: promises, Lenin, the Petrograd Soviet, Trotsky and the Military Revolutionary Committee.
Describe the events of the October Revolution.

topics.title: 3.4 How were the Bolsheviks able to consolidate their power up to 1924?

outcomes.text: Describe Bolshevik policies: Sovnarkom, decrees on rights, workers' control, peace and land, and Brest-Litovsk.
Explain the establishment of dictatorship through the Cheka and closing of the Constituent Assembly.
Explain Bolshevik strengths in the Civil War: leadership, support, geography, organisation and War Communism.
Explain White weaknesses: leadership, conscription, supply and foreign intervention.
Explain the Kronstadt Mutiny's causes, events and impact.
Explain the introduction and impact of the New Economic Policy.

units.title: Paper 3 Historical interpretations: The origins of the First World War

topics.title: Historical interpretations and approaches

outcomes.text: Explain why historians produce different interpretations: fragmentary evidence, selection of evidence, changing views over time and the influence of time and place.
Describe how historians ask different questions and are influenced by ideology and belief.
Explain the inter-relationship between historians' interpretations and approaches.

topics.title: Who or what was to blame for the First World War?

outcomes.text: Describe the context c.1890-1914: Great Power tensions, alliances, militarism, the arms race and Balkan instability.
Describe war plans, the Sarajevo assassination, the July crisis, mobilisation and declarations of war.
Assess how far Great Power tension was likely to lead to war.
Assess how important the decisions of key individuals were.
Explain the impact of Article 231 of the Versailles Treaty on the debate.
Explain how and why the idea of shared responsibility arose, and how the Second World War affected the debate.
Explain the Fischer thesis and the German reaction to it.
Describe challenges to Fischer and modern interpretations blaming nations other than Germany.
Assess the relative importance of long-term and short-term factors.
Explain how the centenary affected the debate and the importance of contingency over motive.

topics.title: 1.1 How did Mussolini gain control of Italy?

subtopics.title: Post-war Italy and the rise of Mussolini

outcomes.text: Explain the problems after the war: war's impact, the Mutilated Victory, Fiume, unemployment, inflation, unstable government and the Biennio Rosso.
Describe Mussolini's appointment in 1922: policy programmes, Fasci di Combattimento, squadrismo and the March on Rome.
Explain the role of Victor Emmanuel III and the elites, and the nature of the National government.
Describe the establishment of dictatorship 1922-26: the Grand Council, Militia, Acerbo Law, Matteotti's murder and powers of the Head of Government.
Assess the extent of fascist control by 1926, including support, opposition and dissent.

topics.title: 1.2 How effectively did Mussolini govern Italy?

outcomes.text: Explain the terror state: OVRA, MVSN, special tribunals and the 1938 antisemitic laws.
Explain propaganda and censorship: links to Ancient Rome, personality cult, Ministry of Popular Culture, media, rallies, art and sport.
Assess the extent and success of propaganda.
Describe fascist institutions and central government: Duce, PNF, Grand Council, king, cabinet, prefects and podestas.
Explain foreign policy aims: prestige, the Mediterranean and African empire.
Describe methods: diplomacy, alliances, Corfu, Albania and Abyssinia, and assess success.

topics.title: 1.3 How successful were Mussolini's economic policies?

outcomes.text: Explain attempts to modernise the economy: aims, Di Stefani, the battles for the lira, grain and marshes, and autarky.
Explain the Great Depression's impact and government intervention through IMI, IRI and public works.
Explain the Corporate State: the Third Way, the Vidoni Pact, Rocco Law, Ministry of Corporations and Charter of Labour.
Assess outcomes of the Corporate State.
Assess living standards: welfare, pay, working hours and consumption.

topics.title: 1.4 How far did Mussolini transform Italian society?

outcomes.text: Explain fascist attitudes to women, the aim to raise the birth rate and limits on women's work.
Describe the Battle for Births and its outcomes.
Explain indoctrination of youth: Gentile's reforms, curriculum, teachers, universities and the ONB.
Explain religious policy: early anti-clericalism, the Lateran Treaties, church support and 1930s tensions.
Explain the impact of the OND and the Reform of Customs.
Assess opposition: strikes, the Communist Party, Justice and Liberty, non-conformity and assassination attempts.

topics.title: 2.1 How did Stalin gain control of the Soviet Union?

outcomes.text: Explain the power vacuum after Lenin's death, collective leadership, Lenin's Testament and funeral.
Compare the strengths and weaknesses of Stalin, Trotsky, Bukharin, Kamenev, Rykov, Tomsky and Zinoviev.
Explain Stalin's use of party roles such as General Secretary.
Explain the ideological differences: NEP versus industrialisation, Socialism in One Country versus Permanent Revolution, and changing alliances.
Explain repression and propaganda to 1929, including the Lenin's disciple cult.

topics.title: 2.2 How effectively did Stalin govern the Soviet Union?

outcomes.text: Explain the reasons for the Terror and Purges, opposition to Stalin and Kirov's murder.
Describe the NKVD, show trials and the Yezhovshchina, gulags and purge of the armed forces.
Describe the development of the Stalin cult and propaganda methods.
Explain the nature of Stalin's leadership and the Stalin Constitution.
Explain relations with Germany and the search for collective security: Comintern, League, France and Czechoslovakia.
Describe intervention in the Spanish Civil War and policy towards China and Japan.
Explain the Nazi-Soviet Pact.

topics.title: 2.3 How successful were Stalin's economic policies?

outcomes.text: Explain the reasons for the Great Turn: security, self-sufficiency, a socialist economy and Stalin's control.
Explain the reasons for collectivisation, voluntary and forced collectivisation, and state farms.
Assess the impact of collectivisation: requisitioning, famine, yields and dekulakisation.
Explain the reasons for industrialisation and the role of Gosplan.
Describe the organisation, aims and results of the first three Five Year Plans.
Describe major projects, industrial centres and the Stakhanovite movement.
Assess urban living and working conditions: wage differentials, incentives, discipline, housing and consumer goods.

topics.title: 2.4 How far did Stalin transform Soviet society?

outcomes.text: Explain the Great Retreat on marriage, divorce and childbirth, and women's opportunities and limits at work.
Describe the treatment of national groups within the Soviet Union.
Describe education reforms and the 1936 reversal of earlier reforms.
Explain the Cultural Revolution and Socialist Realism's aims and impact.
Describe repression of organised religion.
Assess the Church's continued influence on society.

topics.title: 3.1 How did Hitler gain control of Germany?

outcomes.text: Explain Weimar's problems: the Great Depression, the unpopularity of Muller and Bruning, and the rise of communism.
Explain growing Nazi support 1929-32: Hitler's appeal, the SA, propaganda, promises and elite support.
Explain Hitler's appointment in 1933: the 1932 elections, von Schleicher, Hindenburg and von Papen.
Explain consolidation of power 1933-34: the Reichstag Fire, March 1933 election and Enabling Act.
Explain the Night of the Long Knives, Hindenburg's death and the army oath.

topics.title: 3.2 How effectively did the Nazis govern Germany?

outcomes.text: Describe the terror state: Gestapo, block wardens, police and SD, courts, SS and concentration camps.
Describe propaganda: Goebbels, media control, Nuremberg Rallies and the 1936 Olympics.
Assess opposition from youth, the Churches, the left and passive resistance.
Explain foreign policy aims: reversing Versailles, pan-Germanism, Lebensraum and defeating communism.
Describe the methods and steps from leaving the League to Barbarossa, and assess planning and consistency.

topics.title: 3.3 How successful were Nazi economic policies?

outcomes.text: Describe responses to the Depression: Schacht's schemes, Mefo Bills, public works, Reich Labour Service and unemployment law.
Describe agricultural policies: tariffs, the Reich Food Estate and Reich Entailed Farm Law.
Explain rearmament and autarky: the New Plan, Goering's Four Year Plan, war industries and guns or butter.
Assess living standards: employment, hours, pay, the DAF, Strength through Joy and Beauty of Work.

topics.title: 3.4 How far did the Nazis transform German society?

outcomes.text: Explain Nazi views on women's roles (Kinder, Kuche, Kirche), limits on work, birthrate efforts and the post-1937 change.
Describe changes to education and the Hitler Youth and BDM.
Describe religious policy: the Concordat, Reich Church and German Faith Movement.
Explain Nazi race theories: Social Darwinism and eugenics.
Explain other reasons for persecuting Jews, and methods: boycotts, Nuremberg Laws and Kristallnacht.
Describe persecution of other minorities and the reasons for it.
